title_guess: Mutual funds: why small investors pool money, NAV worked out with numbers, close-ended vs open-ended funds on one timeline, AMCs and the five SEBI categories
recurring_cast: fund manager in a tie on an office chair, pulling a red cart of cash bundles labelled MUTUAL FUND (FUND during the pooling scene)
row of six INVESTOR person icons along the top
stock exchange building (columned building with a coloured wash)
'PROFESSIONAL MANAGEMENT' label line feeding the fund manager
fund life timeline bar: launch date, NFO window, maturity date
AMC office building icon (three black towers)
running_examples: NAV: total assets 1 crore, liabilities (fund running costs) 10 lakh, 9 lakh units, so NAV = (1 crore - 10 lakh) / 9 lakh = Rs 10 per unit
Rs 1000 invested at NAV Rs 10 gives 100 units (spoken only, never on screen)
close-ended fund life: launch date -> NFO period (subscribe) -> fixed units traded on the stock market -> maturity date (paid out at NAV, or turns open-ended)

best_moments.why: the six investors each hold a rupee note over an empty red cart; the notes leave them, the cart fills with cash bundles and a fund manager sits down to pull it: pooling small money into one managed fund in one picture
a curved arrow runs from the 'different asset classes' box back into the 'Total Assets: 1 crore' bar under the cart: what the fund bought is what its assets are

green up-arrows rise on the asset classes, on total assets and on NAV in turn, and NAV is boxed inside 'Investment = Units x NAV' with a dotted loop: growth passes along a visible chain to the investor

the close-ended life on one bar: a yellow NFO window, then a long pink 'no new units' stretch, with an arrow carrying the UNITS up into a stock exchange building tagged 'buy/sell only through stock market'

the same timeline is turned into an open-ended fund by taking rules away: the exchange panel dissolves into particles, the 'no new units' line is struck, the bar turns all yellow, 'number of units keep changing' writes on, and 'maturity date' is struck

three fund rows (each manager-plus-cart) stack inside one black frame under an office-building icon, then the frame is titled ASSET MANAGEMENT COMPANY: a company that holds many funds, shown as a container

weak_moments.why: the five fund categories are a blue text list written on line by line for about 100 s; SEBI's rule and the Sensex/Nifty index examples are only spoken, and there is no picture of what each fund holds
the four investor challenges are text labels on lines around a static investor-to-exchange picture; lack of time or expertise is never acted out
the rule that new buyers pay the current NAV, up or down, is spoken over an unchanged frame; the Rs 1000 -> 100 units example is also never shown
what happens at maturity (each investor paid units x current NAV) is spoken while nothing changes on screen
on-screen sentence has a double negative ('no new units ... is not issued'), which says the opposite of the narration if read literally

doubtful fact to check before reuse: the screen says retail investors cannot buy large-ticket instruments like government bonds; retail access to G-secs exists in India (for example RBI's retail direct scheme)
doubtful as stated: 'open-ended fund units do not trade on the stock market'; ETFs, which the video itself lists later, are open-ended and exchange-traded

segments.teaches: a small investor in the stock market faces four problems: no expertise, no time, small amounts that cannot buy large-ticket instruments, and so no diversification, which leaves him exposed to high risk

investor -> 'lack of diversification' -> red 'exposed to the high risk'

segments.notes: 9 change events in 55 s (about every 6 s). The diversification line is a small cause chain (small amount -> no diversification -> high risk). Verify the on-screen claim about retail investors and government bonds before reuse.
segments.idea: investing alone is risky for a small investor because he lacks skill, time and enough money to spread it out

segments.teaches: small investors pool their money into a collective fund and hire a professional manager, who can invest the large pool across asset classes (equity, debt, gold) without any ticket-size limit; this collective fund is a mutual fund

segments.idea: pooling many small amounts and handing them to a professional solves each of the earlier challenges

segments.teaches: NAV (net asset value) = (total assets - liabilities) / number of units; worked example: 1 crore assets, 10 lakh running costs as liabilities, 9 lakh units gives NAV Rs 10, the price of one unit

elements.what: NAV over a cream panel around the cart
green bar 'Total Assets: 1 Crore' under the cart
curved arrow from the asset-classes box (now yellow) back into the total-assets bar
peach bar 'Total Liabilities: 10 Lakh'
green bar 'Total Units: 9 Lakh'
NAV = [1 crore - 10 lakh] / 9 lakh
'= 10 Rs' beside NAV

segments.notes: 9 change events in 84 s (about every 9 s). The diversification line and the small explanation texts drop away (the investor row stays); the three numbers stack as coloured bars under the cart, then the formula and the answer. All four numbers are spoken and shown. 'Liabilities' are the fund's running costs (salary, office rent) in the narration; the bar does not show what they are.
segments.idea: the price of one unit is what the fund owns, minus what it owes, shared over all units
segments.shown_as: NAV titles the cart's panel; a green 'Total Assets 1 crore' bar writes under the cart and a curved arrow loops into it from the asset-classes box; a peach '10 lakh liabilities' bar and a green '9 lakh units' bar stack beneath; the formula writes under them and '= 10 Rs' appears beside the NAV title
segments.example: (1 crore - 10 lakh) / 9 lakh units = Rs 10 NAV

segments.teaches: investors get units for their money (investment = units x NAV); when the assets' value rises, NAV rises and so does the investment; anyone buying new units pays the current NAV, high or low

elements.what: light-blue band under the investor row: investors get UNITS against their investment
'Investment = Units x NAV'

segments.notes: 4 change events in 42 s, none after 222 s. Spoken but not shown: Rs 1000 buys 100 units; new or existing investors buy at the current NAV, up or down (225-241 s, frame unchanged).
segments.idea: your money grows exactly as the NAV grows, because you hold a fixed number of units
segments.shown_as: a blue band 'investors get units' writes under the investor row with 'Investment = Units x NAV' below it; green up-arrows rise on the asset classes, the total-assets bar and NAV one after another; 'if NAV grows, investment grows' appears and NAV in the formula is boxed with a dotted loop

segments.teaches: mutual funds are of two types, open-ended and close-ended; a close-ended fund has a launch date and a maturity date; the launch is the New Fund Offer (NFO), and the NFO period is the only window to subscribe

elements.what: compact 'professional management -> mutual fund' block splitting by two green elbows into OPEN ENDED and CLOSE ENDED
black underline under CLOSE ENDED
long black bar with blue ticks 'Launch Date' and 'Maturity Date'
'New Fund Offer / NFO' with a dotted drop to the launch tick
short yellow band 'NFO Period' at the bar's start
box: time frame when the scheme is open for subscription

segments.notes: 9 change events in 47 s (about every 5 s). The underline acts as a 'you are here' marker on the classification tree; it moves to OPEN ENDED later.
segments.idea: a close-ended fund has a fixed life, and you can join it only in the short window at the start
segments.shown_as: the canvas clears to a small fund block that splits into OPEN ENDED and CLOSE ENDED; CLOSE ENDED is underlined; above it a long bar draws with 'launch date' and 'maturity date' ticks, 'New Fund Offer (NFO)' drops onto the launch tick, a short yellow 'NFO period' band fills the start, and a callout says this is the time to subscribe

segments.teaches: after the NFO a close-ended fund issues no new units and takes no new investors until maturity; the fixed units are listed and traded on the stock market, which is the only way to buy or sell them; at maturity investors are paid by current NAV, or the fund may become open-ended

elements.what: pink band from the NFO end to maturity: no new units issued in this period
blue 'UNITS' over the NFO band
curved arrow from UNITS up to a stock exchange building
pink box: fixed units issued in NFO are listed and traded on the stock market
red 'BUY/SELL only through stock market'
green dotted extension past maturity: after maturity the fund may become open-ended

segments.notes: 4 change events in 70 s (about every 17 s). The pink band's sentence is a double negative on screen. The maturity payout (units x current NAV, 339-349 s) is spoken over an unchanged frame.
segments.idea: once the window closes, the units are fixed; you can only buy them from someone else on the stock exchange
segments.shown_as: a pink band runs from the end of the yellow NFO window to the maturity tick with 'no new units' under it; 'UNITS' sits on the NFO window and a curved arrow carries them up into a stock exchange building with a pink 'listed and traded' box and a red 'buy/sell only through stock market' tag; finally a green dotted line runs on past maturity with 'may become open-ended'

segments.teaches: open-ended funds are not traded on the stock market; the fund can create new units at any time, so investors can enter or exit any time; the number of units keeps changing, and there is no maturity date

'Maturity Date' struck through

segments.notes: 5 change events in 43 s (about every 9 s). Taught by subtraction: the close-ended rules are removed from the same bar one by one. Doubtful as stated: ETFs (listed later) are open-ended and exchange-traded.
segments.idea: an open-ended fund has no closed window, no fixed units and no end date

segments.teaches: SEBI allows mutual funds only in five categories: equity funds, debt funds (corporate and government bonds), hybrid funds (equity and debt), solution-oriented schemes (retirement, children's education, goals), and other schemes (index funds, ETFs, fund of funds); an index fund follows an index like Sensex or Nifty
